If a body loses electrons, its net charge becomes positive.
If it gains electrons, it becomes negative.

Charge adds algebraically, so plus three microcoulombs and minus five

Let's put two stationary point charges in vacuum.
Coulomb's law says the force magnitude is proportional to the product of their

The line joining the charges gives the force direction: like signs repel,

Electric field lets us describe the influence of source charges before choosing
the charge that will feel it.
At a point, the field is force per unit positive test charge, with the test
charge small enough not to disturb the source arrangement.
Its unit is newtons per coulomb.
For a point source, field magnitude is the Coulomb constant times the source
charge magnitude divided by distance squared.
Field points away from a positive source and toward a negative source.
Notice that the field belongs to the source arrangement, not to the sign of the
charge we later place there.
A positive charge feels force along the field; a negative charge feels force
opposite to it.
At twenty centimeters from a positive two microcoulomb source in vacuum, field
magnitude is four hundred and fifty thousand newtons per coulomb, directed
outward.
Place a negative one nanocoulomb test charge there.
Its force magnitude is zero point zero zero zero four five newtons and its
direction is inward.
Field lines indicate the local field direction by their tangent.
They do not cross where a unique nonzero field exists, and they are not
automatically the paths moving particles follow.
To combine several sources, add field vectors first, then multiply by the
chosen test charge.
Two equal opposite charges can produce a strong field between them even though
their total net charge is zero.
Total charge alone doesn't determine the field at every point.
Take equal positive and negative charges separated by distance d.
Together they form an electric dipole.
Its dipole moment has magnitude q times the full separation, and its direction
is from the negative charge to the positive charge.
In a uniform external field, the positive charge feels a force along the field
while the negative charge feels an equal force opposite to it.
Net force is zero, but if the dipole is tilted these forces act along different
lines.
They create a torque.
Its magnitude is dipole moment times field times sine of the angle between
them, and the vector form is p cross E.
The torque tends to align the dipole with the field.
For charges of two nanocoulombs separated by one centimeter, dipole moment is
two times ten to the minus eleven coulomb meters.
In a uniform field of one hundred thousand newtons per coulomb at thirty
degrees, torque is one times ten to the minus six newton meters.
Both aligned and opposite alignment give zero torque, but aligned orientation
is stable and opposite alignment is unstable.
Zero torque alone doesn't prove stability.
Far from the dipole compared with its separation, its axial field magnitude is
